newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait agrees U.S. deployment to bolster buildup.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait agrees U.S. deployment to bolster buildup.

text.p: Kuwait on Monday approved a U.S. request to deploy additional ground troops in the Gulf Arab state to expand a U.S. military buildup aimed at deterring former occupier Iraq.

"There was unanimous approval of all of the arrangements proposed by the United States to Kuwait that would preserve security and stability," Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah told a news conference.
Sheikh Saud emphasised repeatedly that Kuwait had felt no hesitation in approving the deployment.
"We would go to any extent to guarantee the security of Kuwait and to prevent the repetition of the 1990 (Iraqi) invasion," he said.
The go-ahead ended a brief misunderstanding with Washington over a premature U.S. announcement of the deployment made prior to Kuwaiti approval.
The U.S. embassy said Kuwait has officially notified the United States of its decision to allow in more U.S. troops.

"We have been officially notified of the approval by Kuwait for the deployment of additional U.S. troops in Kuwait," a U.S. embassy spokesperson said by telephone. The spokesperson did not disclose the number of the troops.

The Clinton administration on Friday announced it had ordered 5,000 army troops from Fort Hood, Texas to join forces already in the Gulf in preparation for possible military action against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
Some U.S. commentators had interpreted the apparent delay in obtaining Kuwaiti approval of the move as reluctance by a close ally to accept American military help.

Diplomats said there no delay because, in what diplomats called an embarrassing gaffe of protocol by U.S. officials, the request was not transmitted to Kuwait until Sunday at a meeting between U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry and the emir, Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah.

The latest crisis between the United States and Iraq started 16 days ago. Washington punished Iraq for intervening in Kurdish factional fighting in northern Iraq by launching 44 cruise missiles at air defence systems in southern Iraq on September 3 and 4.
Diplomats said the additional ground troops from Fort Hood, Texas would be seen as a defensive force, in contrast to the deployment on Friday in Kuwait of U.S. Stealth bombers.
"It's one thing to send in ground troops -- a few thousand men are not going to be able to invade Iraq. It can easily be presented as a defensive measure," one envoy said.
"But it's quite another to send in strike aircraft that can fly all the way to Baghdad."

Diplomats said Saudi Arabia, Washington's most powerful Gulf ally and one of the three states Perry visited on Sunday, was unlikely to back more attacks against Iraq or approve of a continuing American military buildup in the oil-rich region.
"If the United States retaliates once more against Iraq without serious provocation I don't think it would be understood by the international community," a senior Western diplomat in Kuwait said.

U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Madeleine Albright said in the United States on Sunday Washington would not be pressed into "overreacting" to Iraq, and Iraq appeared unlikely to do anything that would provoke a new U.S. attack.
But in Kuwait Perry dismissed Iraq's pledge to abandon attacks on warplanes patrolling southern and northern no-fly zones, saying: "We cannot rely on Saddam Hussein's promises."
